tldr: Coding agents, where large language models (LLMs) write robot control code, tend to ignore obstacles and collide with them even when instructed otherwise in prompts. This paper introduces SafeHarness, an approach that incorporates pre-execution route verification/replanning and collision-free contact behaviors as external tools (harnesses). Without any additional model training, it achieves both high task success and strong safety.
hero_caption: Overview of the concept and performance of SafeHarness. Conventional coding agents frequently collide with obstacles along transit routes or during grasping and placing despite explicit instructions. SafeHarness introduces two external harnesses—for route planning and contact execution—greatly boosting both task success and collision avoidance rates.
overview:
Recently, coding agents that let LLMs write robot control code in Python have attracted widespread attention. They offer a powerful framework capable of orchestrating complex behaviors without task-specific training. Yet an important question remained overlooked: are they truly safe?

When evaluated on benchmarks that require avoiding obstacles, existing agents collided with obstacles in most trials, even though they understood and restated the prompt instructions. The agents treated task completion as their sole objective, neglecting safety constraints. A closer analysis revealed that perception was not the culprit. Instead, the failure stemmed from planning: the agents lacked the notion of generating a clearing route to avoid obstacles, could not replan once stuck, and disregarded safety constraints during contact-rich moments like grasping and placing.

To close this gap, the authors propose SafeHarness. Without altering the underlying model weights, this approach equips the agent with two external tools (harnesses) to support safe execution. The first is obstacle-aware route planning, which grounds scene objects as bounding boxes and verifies/replans waypoint sequences to ensure clearance. The second is obstacle-aware contact execution, which selects the robot gripper's approach direction and orientation based on obstacle locations.

Evaluated on SafeLIBERO, a benchmark designed to assess safety constraints, SafeHarness achieved a 71.9% task success rate and an 87.5% collision avoidance rate. This substantially outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods and delivers a dramatic improvement over the unharnessed baseline, achieving roughly $2.3	imes$ the success rate and $1.5	imes$ the collision avoidance rate.
contributions: Rigorously evaluated coding agents under safety constraints for the first time, identifying the root cause of why prompt instructions alone fail to prevent collisions.
Proposed SafeHarness, a framework consisting of two external tools that treats safety constraints on par with task completion without retraining the model.

Constructed a cooperative mechanism combining a route-planning harness (offline verification and online replanning) and a contact-execution harness (steering approach angles away from obstacles during grasping and placing).
Achieved a 71.9% task success rate and an 87.5% collision avoidance rate on the SafeLIBERO benchmark, significantly outperforming existing SOTA and safety-filter baselines.

sections.heading: Coding agents excel at manipulation, but collisions were everywhere
sections.summary: Coding agents that write control code using LLMs show high versatility, but their safety has never been evaluated. Experiments show that even with clear instructions, agents ignore obstacles, take the shortest path, and repeatedly cause collisions.
sections.details:
Coding agents, which prompt large language models (LLMs) to write programs that call robot control APIs, are advancing rapidly. Without requiring robot-specific reinforcement learning or imitation learning, they have become capable of zero-shot execution on complex pick-and-place tasks.

However, prior research has only evaluated whether the task succeeded, leaving safety—such as what the robot collided with along the way—unmeasured. In the real world, collisions can lead directly to hardware damage or human injury. Collecting more data does not readily solve this; reports indicate that even a tenfold increase in collision-free demonstrations only reduces collision rates by a few percent.

When the authors evaluated existing agents on a benchmark with safety constraints, the findings were striking. Eager to achieve the goal, the agents collided with obstacles in most cases. Examining their reasoning traces revealed that they correctly recognized the obstacles, and the prompts explicitly instructed them not to touch them. Yet, once generating code, the safety constraints were pushed aside.

Decomposing the failures revealed two main causes. First, during transit along routes through the air, the agents could not generate clearing detours and instead rushed along the shortest path. Second, during contact moments when grasping or placing objects, they ignored safety constraints altogether. Swapping in smarter models did not fix this. This motivated the development of SafeHarness, an external framework to guide agents safely.

captions.F1: Safety challenges in coding agents and the effect of introducing SafeHarness. Relying solely on instructions (w/o SafeHarness) leads to collisions during transit routes and contact execution. Introducing the two harnesses elevates safety constraints to first-class objectives, achieving high success and collision avoidance rates.

sections.heading: How does it differ from VLAs, motion planners, and safety filters?
sections.summary: This work sets itself apart from learned VLAs, motion planning, and post-hoc safety filters. Rather than correcting actions after they are generated, it embeds safety directly into the decision-making process before code is executed.
sections.details:
### From VLAs and world models to coding agents
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and world action models, which output joint commands directly from images and language instructions, can only act within the distribution of their training data. Furthermore, their black-box nature makes debugging difficult. In contrast, coding agents output executable Python programs. This provides strong task transferability and allows humans or systems to inspect and edit code before execution.

### The lineage of coding agents in robot manipulation
Starting from Code as Policies, this paradigm evolved through self-correction loops, skill accumulation, and pairing cutting-edge frontier models with fixed VLAs (low-level control policies). However, all previous efforts focused exclusively on task success. None directly addressed safety, often resulting in linear motions straight through obstacles.

### Distinctions from safe control in robotics
Traditional motion planning techniques, such as RRT and CHOMP, generate static trajectories before execution and struggle to adapt to dynamic environmental changes. On the other hand, runtime safety filters using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) intervene and modify hazardous commands on the fly, but they cannot execute fundamental strategic shifts, such as circling around to grasp an object from the opposite side.

This paper takes a distinct stance. Instead of stopping unsafe motions after the fact with a filter, it is the first to embed safety directly into the decision-making stage of coding agents without requiring any model retraining.

sections.heading: Two harnesses for safety: Route verification and contact adaptation
sections.summary: Manipulation is decomposed into free-space transit and contact phases. For transit, the system verifies paths using bounding boxes and replans online. For contact, it determines safe approach directions and wrist orientations based on obstacle proximity.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Preliminaries and problem decomposition
Robot manipulation naturally decomposes into free-space transit (routes) and the contact-rich operations (contacts) that conclude them. Obstacle collisions can occur in both, but the nature of the hazard differs. Routes sweep across wide workspaces, allowing detours, whereas contacts involve fine movements immediately adjacent to the target object, making it impossible to stay far away. SafeHarness therefore addresses safety constraints by handling routes and contacts separately.

### 3.2 Obstacle-Aware Route Planning
Once a robot arm starts moving, a collision cannot be undone. To prevent this, the authors adopted a plan-verify-execute cycle where only validated plans are executed.
- **Spatial perception and route proposals**: First, a segmentation model (SAM-3) detects target objects and obstacles as 3D bounding boxes. Using this information, the LLM proposes candidate routes as sequences of waypoints that steer clear of obstacles. Because moving with an empty gripper requires different clearance than carrying a grasped object, routes are planned anew for each phase.
- **Verification via external module**: Candidate routes produced by the LLM are checked geometrically by an external verifier outside the LLM. If a trajectory intersects an obstacle bounding box, it is immediately rejected, prompting the LLM to replan.
- **Online replanning and context efficiency**: Even if a route passes verification, the robot stops and triggers online replanning from its current state if it gets unexpectedly close to an obstacle or gets stuck during execution. Furthermore, feeding images at every step causes the LLM's context window to explode, degrading reasoning quality. To prevent this, the harness caps the number of visual route-planning queries.

### 3.3 Obstacle-Aware Contact Execution
Even if route planning brings the arm directly above the target (pre-grasp pose), lowering the gripper to grasp can still cause a collision with a nearby obstacle. The system performs an adjacency test between the target object and the obstacle. If an obstacle is adjacent, the gripper selects an approach direction furthest from the obstacle. If no suitable approach direction exists, it rotates the wrist so the gripper's opening axis is tangential (parallel) to the obstacle, lowering vertically from directly above to avoid lateral collisions.

### 3.4 Discussion: Why do agents forget instructions?
Why do capable LLMs fail to obey instructions? The authors attribute this to long-context degradation. Robot manipulation spans hundreds of steps, accumulating tens of thousands of tokens across tool calls and image histories. The initial instruction—"do not touch the obstacle"—gets buried far back in the context, triggering the well-known tendency of LLMs to lose track of early instructions in long prompts. Relying on prompt memory alone is insufficient; constraints must be enforced externally by the tools (harnesses) invoked at each step.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of SafeHarness. Tasks are segmented into phases delineated by contact events. ❶ In route planning, candidate paths are validated against bounding boxes, triggering replanning if rejected or if clearance is breached during execution. ❷ In contact execution, the system checks obstacle adjacency and chooses an approach from the safe, far side.

sections.heading: Benchmark results: Harnesses matter more than model scale
sections.summary: On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, SafeHarness reached a 71.9% task success rate and an 87.5% collision avoidance rate, substantially outperforming prior SOTA. Ablations demonstrate that enforcing constraints via harnesses is far more decisive than raw model intelligence.
sections.details:
### Experimental setup and baselines
The evaluations used the SafeLIBERO benchmark, which places obstacles (pots, boxes, bottles, etc.) across 32 LIBERO tasks. Tasks are split into Level I, where obstacles sit right next to the target object, and Level II, where obstacles obstruct transit routes. The evaluation applies a strict threshold: moving an obstacle by even 1 mm counts as a collision. Using GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 (Astra) as backbones, SafeHarness was compared against a standalone fixed VLA ($\pi_{0.5}$) and AEGIS, a prior safety-filter approach.

### Key results
The findings were unequivocal. Standalone $\pi_{0.5}$ scored a task success rate (TSR) of 57.8% but a collision avoidance rate (CAR) of only 17.1%. While AEGIS raised CAR to 68.9% using safety filters, its success rate plateaued because it overly restricted robot motions. In contrast, SafeHarness with GPT-6 achieved a **TSR of 71.9% (+6.5 points over previous SOTA) and a CAR of 87.5% (+27.0 points)**, establishing dominant records on both metrics. Because it actively seeks safe paths rather than abandoning actions for safety, task success increases alongside safety.

### Insights from ablations
An intriguing finding emerged when scaling the language model from GPT-5.5 to GPT-6. Without harnesses, scaling improved Level I safety (local grasp orientation decisions) but produced virtually no improvement on Level II (long-range detour routes). Visual reasoning can improve localized judgments, but memory alone cannot sustain long-range trajectory safety.

However, once equipped with SafeHarness, both GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 saw CAR jump above 85%, largely erasing the performance gap between models. This demonstrates that **safety is guaranteed not by the raw intelligence of the LLM, but by the external harness**.

### Qualitative analysis
In a task requiring orange juice to be placed into a basket, the unharnessed agent noted in its initial reasoning that it must avoid a bottle, yet it took the shortest path during execution and knocked the bottle over. In contrast, SafeHarness planned and verified waypoints that detoured around the obstacle bounding box, safely completing the task without collisions.

captions.F3: Comparison of rollouts on SafeLIBERO. In the top row (w/o SafeHarness), the agent recognizes the wine bottle but moves along the shortest path, knocking it over. In the bottom row (with SafeHarness), verified route planning detours around the yellow bounding box, cleanly completing the task with zero collisions.

sections.heading: Prompts are not constraints: Place guards where the robot moves
sections.summary: Obstacle avoidance hinges on the geometric relationship between obstacles and the task, not model scale. Because LLMs cannot reliably sustain safety constraints from prompts alone, safety mechanisms must be built directly into the tools driving physical execution.
sections.details:
The conclusion drawn from this study is highly practical: instructions given to LLMs do not function as strict constraints. Constraints must exist where the robot physically moves—within the harness.

If an obstacle lies on a transit route, free-space paths must be geometrically verified; if an obstacle sits adjacent to a target, grasp directions and wrist postures must be adjusted. By implementing these two physical requirements as external harnesses, the authors demonstrated that safe autonomous control can be achieved with a frozen VLA without any gradient updates or additional training.

### Limitations and future work
The paper candidly outlines several limitations. To match the SafeLIBERO evaluation suite, obstacles are treated as single rectangular bounding boxes, requiring further extensions for environments with multiple cluttered obstacles. In addition, contact heuristics are tuned specifically for parallel-jaw grippers. Finally, the geometric verification and online replanning require several minutes of planner inference time per episode, and evaluations remain primarily centered on simulation.

takeaways: Do not assume LLMs will respect safety constraints just because they are written in the prompt; constraints are easily forgotten as dialogue history grows.
The fastest path to safety is not expensive model retraining, but attaching stateless geometric verification tools as external harnesses.
Decomposing manipulation constraints into two distinct phases—transit route clearance and contact approach direction—provides a clear, modular design.
Proactively planning only safe alternatives preserves task success far better than rejecting or suppressing actions post-hoc using safety filters like CBFs.
limitations: Obstacles are modeled as single rectangular bounding boxes, requiring extensions to handle multiple obstacles and complex geometries.
Contact avoidance heuristics are specifically designed for standard parallel-jaw grippers.
Repeated verification and replanning introduce test-time compute overhead, requiring several minutes of inference time per episode.
Evaluations were conducted primarily in simulation (SafeLIBERO), leaving validation under real-world sensor noise and dynamic obstacles for future work.
